working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Courses
angle: A practical, opinionated guide to deciding between an electric and a push trolley that is grounded in the specific realities of UK golf: hilly heathland, muddy links winters, small car boots, and the question of whether the premium is genuinely worth it for how often most club golfers actually play. Rather than listing every model on the market, the post helps the reader arrive at the right category first, then points them at what to look for within it.
research_notes:
- Electric trolleys use a battery-powered motor so the golfer walks alongside and steers rather than pushing; this conserves energy across a full round (source: trolleyguru.co.uk)
- Push trolleys require the golfer to do all the work but are lighter, cheaper, and typically include more storage on the handle console than electric equivalents (source: golfmonthly.com, todays-golfer.com)
- Old-style pull trolleys (single-handle, dragged behind) put strain on one side of the body and are worth discouraging; push (two-handle, three-wheel) is the modern standard for manual use (source: todays-golfer.com)
- Electric models are heavier due to battery and motor hardware, so a compact fold matters more with electric than with push, since you are lifting more weight into the boot (source: trolleyguru.co.uk)
- Battery sizing matters for UK conditions: an 18-hole lithium battery covers a standard round; 27- or 36-hole batteries suit hillier courses or back-to-back rounds (source: trolleyguru.co.uk)
- Downhill Control (DHC) is a feature on some Motocaddy models (e.g. S1 DHC, M1 DHC) that automatically regulates speed on descents, genuinely useful on hilly UK parkland and heathland courses (source: golfgear360.co.uk)
- Push trolleys better suited to flatter courses; electric motors particularly earn their cost on hilly terrain (source: golfmonthly.com, trolleyguru.co.uk)
- Follow/remote electric trolleys (e.g. Stewart Golf Q Follow uses Bluetooth to follow the golfer hands-free) sit at the premium end and suit golfers who want the closest thing to a caddy experience (source: golf-gear.co.uk, moresports.com)
- Key brands active in UK market 2026: Motocaddy, PowaKaddy (founded 1983, based in Sittingbourne, Kent), Stewart Golf, Big Max, Clicgear, Hill Billy
- Push trolley standouts in 2026 coverage: Big Max Blade IP 2 (FlatFold mechanism, lightweight), Motocaddy Cube Push (compact), PowaKaddy DLX-Lite FF, Stewart R1-S (UK-made, aerospace-grade aluminium frame), Clicgear 4.0
- Electric standouts in 2026 coverage: Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote (remote control, touchscreen GPS), PowaKaddy FX and CT ranges, Motocaddy S1/M1 (entry-level), Stewart Golf Q Follow (follow-me Bluetooth)
- Push trolleys easier to transport and store due to lighter, more compact folded size; electric trolleys slightly larger but modern designs fold down significantly smaller than older generations (source: golfmonthly.com)
- Budget guidance: electric trolleys carry a significantly higher price tag and are generally most practical for golfers who play regularly enough to justify the outlay, though entry-level electric options exist for those making the step up (source: golfmonthly.com)
- The MGI E-Boost Push Cart is noted as a hybrid option sitting between traditional push and electric categories (source: golfmonthly.com)
- NOTE: specific prices from search results vary by source and may not be reliable; do not state specific prices in the post body. Describe cost tiers in general terms only.
must_avoid:

- Do not fabricate or invent quotes from reviewers, brands, or pros
- No medical or injury claims beyond the well-known general point that pulling a single-arm trolley puts uneven strain on the body
- No affiliate links to any product not in the approved-partners list; mention brands and models informationally only where not approved
